canonical_statement: The study asks how reliable an LLM judge must be for a threshold-based skill-retirement rule to remain informative in a self-evolving skill library.
The study defines library drift, proposes the Ratchet controller, derives its non-divergence conditions, and tests the predicted sensor-failure boundaries experimentally.
Library drift is defined as a round in which expected held-out pass@1 with the current skill set is lower than expected pass@1 from the same frozen model with skill injection withheld.
Ratchet uses one frozen model in five roles—Router, Solver, Critic, Synthesizer, and Curator—over a shared append-only evidence log.
The Router returns at most one active skill or declines, so each graded outcome is attributable either to one named skill or to the bare model.
For each active skill, the Curator computes measured contribution as (passes minus failures) divided by routed trials, equivalently c-hat(s)=2 p-hat(s)-1.
Default contribution-based eviction requires both at least 100 routed trials and measured contribution at or below -0.10.
The active shelf is capped at 50 skills by default, and when synthesis overflows the cap the active skill with the lowest measured contribution is evicted.
A suite-level authoring prior constrains synthesized skills to reusable patterns with an applicability condition, key insight, known pitfalls, and a post-condition check.
Near-duplicate failure-pattern labels are canonicalized by union-find over embedding cosine similarity at 0.85, and synthesis requires an uncovered cluster of at least three patterns.
Rollback is triggered after held-out pass@1 remains more than 0.10 below the running best for five consecutive rounds, restoring the best shelf snapshot.

Proposition 1 states that, under unbiased and consistent per-skill contribution estimates and a uniform concentration guarantee, expected pass@1 is bounded below by the no-skill control minus the eviction margin, estimation error, and a C-delta union-bound term.

The paper argues that the Proposition 1 floor is finite because the active width C and eviction margin tau are finite; without either quantity the corresponding open-loop guarantee is not informative.
Judge error is modeled as a binary channel with failure-to-pass rate rho_F_to_P, pass-to-failure rate rho_P_to_F, and kappa=1-rho_F_to_P-rho_P_to_F greater than zero.
Under symmetric judge noise below 0.5, scored pass rates contract toward 0.5 while preserving ordering, and the evidence floor must grow in proportion to (1-2 rho)^-2 to resolve the contracted means.
Eviction is informative only when the true pass-rate ceiling p-star=(pi_tau-rho_F_to_P)/kappa lies strictly between zero and one.
When rho_F_to_P reaches pi_tau=(1-tau)/2, no skill is evictable in expectation at any sample size because the eviction condition becomes unsatisfiable even for a skill with zero true pass rate.
When rho_P_to_F reaches 1-pi_tau, the eviction rule becomes indiscriminate in the opposite direction, making every skill evictable in expectation.
The paper concludes that increasing sample size can reduce estimation error but cannot correct a false-pass bias that displaces the eviction statistic across its threshold.
The main benchmark uses a fixed MBPP+/100 slice of 100 tasks, split into 60 train tasks and 40 held-out evaluation tasks, restricted to tasks the frozen base model fails on at least one probe seed.

canonical_statement: The offline judge audit injects one defect per class into citation-grounded report sections: five mechanically check-visible defect classes and two semantic classes (claim negation and number swap).
The deterministic audit component used 155 report sections for the check-visible defect classes; claim negation was available in 137 sections.

canonical_statement: The deterministic grader had recall 1.00 on all five check-visible defect classes, 0.00 on claim negation, and 0.05 on number swap.
The held-out judge flagged number-swap defects at 0.985 and claim-negation defects at 0.927.

population.label: Paired clean and injected sections assessed by held-out judge

canonical_statement: The corruption sweep uses RPT/71 as the main reference-free testbed, repeats the false-pass-bias arm on RPT/58, RPT/133, and MBPP+/100, and corrupts training reward only while evaluation uses the true grader.
The corruption sweep uses tau=0.10, Nmin=24, C=12, three seeds, and therefore pi_tau=0.45.
On RPT/71, clean reward produced 1.333 genuine contribution-based retirements per run and 22.0 skills written.
Across tested symmetric-noise rates 0.10 through 0.40 on RPT/71, genuine retirements remained between 0.667 and 1.000 per run versus 1.333 under the clean grader.

At the default false-pass boundary rho_F_to_P=0.45, RPT/71 had 0.333 genuine retirements per run, 15.7 skills written, and a held-out pass@1 change of -0.065 versus the clean loop.

canonical_statement: The audited judge condition produced 10.333 genuine retirements per run, 19.0 skills written, realized reward divergence 0.591, and a held-out pass@1 change of +0.024 versus clean.
Symmetric reward noise did not reduce held-out evaluation quality at any tested rate on RPT/71; the authors treat the small positive differences as absence of harm rather than evidence of benefit.
The downstream harm from false-pass bias was non-monotonic: evaluation was worst near the theoretical boundary and recovered when stronger bias also starved synthesis.

Across the full corruption sweep, all mean evaluation scores stayed within 0.125 pass@1 of the no-skill control, consistent with the bounded-width non-divergence role even where contribution eviction was disabled.

canonical_statement: The injected corruption channel is exogenous; the study does not cover a coupled regime in which the evolving library changes judge error rates over time by exploiting the judge’s blind spots.
The offline audit certifies only enumerable defect classes that the operator can name, not all possible failure modes of a reference-free judge.
Measured contribution is associational and routed-conditional, with survivorship and selection confounding because the Router steers skills toward tasks on which they already appear useful.
The load-bearing MBPP+ experiments use three seeds, while the six additional model-family probes are single-seed and are presented only as a generality signal.
The study does not perform a head-to-head governance bake-off against other skill-lifecycle curators on a shared evidence log.

The authors state that the two propositions apply to any artifact store that retires entries by thresholding one scalar per artifact, including memory banks, retrieval corpora, and score-pruned tool registries.
The paper recommends auditing both judge error directions before enabling lifecycle governance, because a controller can be disabled while end-task scores move little or non-monotonically.
The paper provides a project repository for Ratchet at the GitHub URL listed on the title page.
The paper reports prior SkillsBench findings that LLM-authored skills were +0.0 percentage points over a no-skill control while human-authored skills were +16.2 percentage points.
